newsitem.title: GERMANY: Details of Germany coal subsidy compromise.
newsitem.headline: Details of Germany coal subsidy compromise.

text.p: A compromise on coal subsidies reached on Thursday would offer higher state aid to Germany's 18 pits up to the year 2000 than originally planned by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.

Under a deal struck by Bonn, miners leaders, coal producers and the country's two coal-mining states, total coal aid would rise next year to 9.25 billion marks from 8.9 billion this year and then fall back to 8.5 billion in 2000.
Aid would then slide more sharply to 5.5 billion marks by 2005 -- the level originally planned by Kohl.
But the fine-print of the deal shows that Bonn will eventually end up paying more in subsidies than the 3.8 billion marks in 2005 than the figure the government had indicated.
Extra payments in that year, for example, would take that figure nearer to 4.2 billion.
Following is a breakdown of who pays what between 1997 and 2005 (figures in billions of marks):
NOTE - Federal government total includes payments 200 million marks a year from 1998 on behalf of Saarland state, as long as the state takes a 26 percent stake in Saarbergwerke AG.

Bonn will also make extra annual payments of 300 million marks a year from 1998, as long as North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) coal producer Ruhrkohle takes over the rest of Saarbergwerke. NRW will take over half those payments from 2001.
Coal industry payments of 200 marks a year from 2001 on would come out of non-mining profits at Ruhrkohle.
